claim: P@10 = 0.45 on the 10 test items (agent-drafted labels, pending human review)

random_expected.how: expected P@10 of a uniformly random order of all candidates = judged-relevant / candidates
expected P@10 of a uniformly random order of all candidates = judged-relevant / candidates

fixed.trust: constant here (every seed row is L0)
fixed.past_results: constant here (no metrics for seed rows)

pooling.method: TREC-style: union of the top 20 from recommender_default, bm25_only and relevance_only (round 1), plus the tuned recommender's top 10 (round 2+)
pooling.bias_disclosure: Unjudged pairs count as not relevant. At depth 10 the pooled systems are judged to 100% (lowest judged@10 on test), so their P@10 is what full judgement of their top 10 gives. The random baseline was not pooled: most of its picks are unjudged and score 0, so its value is a lower bound and the gap to it is overstated. A destination no pooled system ranked in its top 20 was never judged; if it is relevant, recall is lower than the pool suggests, but P@10 of the pooled systems is unaffected. The rubric, the content items, the recommender and the draft labels were all written by the same agent; the format and rules tests in the rubric are also hard filters in the recommender, which favours it over the baselines. A human review of the labels is needed before this number is claimed.
